meta.tagline: Duolingo won't teach you this — Stockholm edition (what you actually hear).

categories.title: Ordering a beer/food like a local (Sweden)
categories.description: Q → A → what they'll probably say

exchanges.speaker: them

situation.en: The bartender wants to see ID before serving you.

exchanges.notes: Sweden IDs hard: 18 to drink in a bar, 20 to buy at Systembolaget. "Leg" is short for legitimation.

situation.en: You walk in with friends and can't tell if you seat yourselves.

question.es: Kan vi sitta var som helst?

situation.en: You want to know what's on draft before you commit to an order.

question.en: What have you got on tap?

exchanges.speaker: them

situation.en: You're at a Swedish bar and the bartender asks what you want.

question.es: Vad får det lov att vara?

answers.en: A large strong beer, please — 50cl, over 5%.

exchanges.notes: The bartender opens with this. "En stor stark" is what most people order — a 50cl beer over 5%, so it is bigger and stronger than a default pint, not a plain one.

situation.en: You've ordered a beer and they ask how you want it.

likelyReply.es: Vilken vill du ha? / Nån särskild?
likelyReply.en: Which one do you want? / Any specific one?

situation.en: The bartender asks whether you want food as well.

question.es: Vill du ha något att äta också?

likelyReply.en: Here you go. / That'll be [AMOUNT] SEK.

exchanges.speaker: them

situation.en: You're paying and they ask how.

exchanges.notes: Cash is genuinely rare and plenty of Swedish bars refuse it outright. Swish is the local phone-to-phone app and needs a Swedish bank.

situation.en: You've paid and they ask whether you want a receipt.

items.en: Is Swish okay? (only relevant with friends and some places)
Cheers! — with eye contact, every single time.
The default Swedish order: a large strong lager.
A warmer thank you than a plain tack.
Can we share? — splitting plates is completely normal.
That's everything, thanks — closing an order.

exchanges.speaker: them

situation.en: A colleague or friend suggests coffee in the middle of the afternoon.

question.en: Shall we go for a fika?

exchanges.notes: Fika is coffee, something sweet and sitting down — all three. Declining is fine; proposing a time instead is better.

situation.en: The buns behind the glass aren't labelled.

question.es: Vad är det för bullar idag?
question.en: What buns have you got today?

situation.en: Everything in the counter is sweet and you'd rather have something else.

question.en: Do you have anything without sugar?

situation.en: You're at the counter of a café and know what you want.

question.es: En kaffe och en kanelbulle, tack.
question.en: A coffee and a cinnamon bun, please.

situation.en: They ring you up and need to know whether you're staying.
You want to check the refill won't appear on the bill.

answers.en: Yes, as much as you like.

exchanges.speaker: them

situation.en: Your cup is empty and someone comes round with the pot.

exchanges.notes: Påtår is the free second cup and it really is free. A third one is a tretår.

exchanges.speaker: you

situation.en: You're getting up from the table you shared with someone.

exchanges.notes: Said to whoever you sat with, every time. Leaving without it reads as cold.

categories.title: Starting a convo/basic survival (Stockholm)
categories.description: Q → A → what they'll probably say

exchanges.speaker: them

situation.en: Someone greets you.

exchanges.notes: "Tja" is the casual Stockholm hello.

situation.en: Someone asks how you're doing.
You need help and want to check whether they speak English.
You didn't catch what someone just said.

likelyReply.es: Jag kan säga det på engelska.
likelyReply.en: I can say it in English.

exchanges.speaker: you

situation.en: They answered at full Swedish speed and you need it slower.

question.en: Could you speak a little more slowly?

exchanges.notes: Swedes switch to English the moment they hear you struggle. This is the sentence that keeps them in Swedish.

situation.en: You don't know a word and want to ask what it is.

question.en: How do you say [WORD] in Swedish?

situation.en: You're looking for a place and stop someone to ask.

answers.es: Där borta. / Rakt fram. / Till vänster/höger.
answers.en: Over there. / Straight ahead. / To the left/right.

likelyReply.es: Det är nära. / Det tar typ [ANTAL] minuter.
likelyReply.en: It's close. / It takes about [NUMBER] minutes.

exchanges.speaker: them

situation.en: Someone you've just met is leaving and says you'll be in touch.

exchanges.notes: Usually means nothing will happen. Say it back, mean it as much as they did, and take no offence.

exchanges.speaker: them

situation.en: Somebody you've just met asks what you're called.

exchanges.notes: Heter is the verb for being called, so it is jag heter, never jag är for a name.

exchanges.speaker: them

situation.en: Two lines in, they want to know where you've come from.

exchanges.notes: Var kommer du ifrån? and varifrån kommer du? are the same question. Answer with ifrån and you sound like you have said it before.

exchanges.speaker: them

situation.en: They have switched into Swedish and you have to say how little you have.

likelyReply.es: Ingen fara, vi tar det på engelska.
likelyReply.en: No problem, we'll do it in English.

exchanges.notes: Swedes switch to English the second they hear you struggle. Jag pratar inte svenska is the honest version; jag lär mig svenska keeps them in Swedish a little longer.

situation.en: Somebody wants to know what you're doing in the country.

answers.es: Ja, jag är här på semester.

likelyReply.es: Då har du tur med vädret.
likelyReply.en: You're lucky with the weather, then.

situation.en: They ask how much of the trip you have left.

likelyReply.es: Då hinner du med Gamla stan.
likelyReply.en: You'll have time for Gamla stan, then.

exchanges.speaker: them

situation.en: The talk turns to what you do for a living.

question.en: What do you do for work?

exchanges.notes: Vad jobbar du med? is what a Swede actually asks, and it comes later in the evening than it would at home: work is not the opening question here.

exchanges.speaker: them

situation.en: Somebody at the table asks your age straight out.

exchanges.notes: Jag är trettio år gammal is correct and almost nobody says all of it. Drop år gammal and give the number.

exchanges.speaker: you

situation.en: You've answered six questions in a row and want to ask one.

question.es: Och du då? Vad gör du?
question.en: And you? What do you do?

exchanges.notes: Och du då? is the standard turn-it-around. A question answered and not returned reads as you being finished talking.

exchanges.speaker: them

situation.en: Someone who fed you a month ago greets you with this.

answers.en: Thank you too — it was fun!

likelyReply.en: We should do it again soon.

exchanges.notes: Said the next time you meet anyone who hosted you, however long ago. There is no English for it, and not saying it is noticed.

exchanges.speaker: them

situation.en: You've just stepped into someone's flat.

question.es: Du kan ta av dig skorna där.
question.en: You can leave your shoes there.

exchanges.notes: Shoes off indoors, all year, no exceptions and no discussion. Take them off before you're asked.

situation.en: You've been invited to someone's home for the evening.

exchanges.speaker: them

situation.en: You've been standing at a counter and someone points at the machine.

question.en: Have you taken a queue ticket?

exchanges.notes: Ticket queues run everything from the pharmacy to the deli counter. Standing in line without one gets you nowhere at all.

exchanges.speaker: you

situation.en: The bus is filling up and the seat beside someone is the last one.

exchanges.notes: On a half-empty bus Swedes spread out. Sitting beside a stranger while seats are free is the odd move, not the polite one.

exchanges.speaker: them

situation.en: A Swedish friend invites you over on a Friday evening.

answers.en: I'd love to — what shall I bring?

likelyReply.en: Just crisps — we'll do the rest.

exchanges.notes: Friday cosiness: sofa, tacos, television. A real national institution, with its own name and its own crisps.

exchanges.speaker: them

situation.en: You've suggested meeting up and get this back.

exchanges.notes: Swedish for no, most of the time. Ask once more and you'll get a straight answer; ask twice and you won't.

exchanges.speaker: you

situation.en: You're pouring someone a drink and want to check the amount.

exchanges.notes: Lagom is the national value: not too much, not too little. Used about a measure, it is a compliment.

note.es: Slang level: medium → heavy. Items marked young are more common among younger people and online.
note.en: If you want to sound local but safe, stick to the ones without a young badge.

phrases.en: Short for bara — "just", often as filler.
To follow / to catch on — slangier than fatta.
Can't be bothered / don't have the energy.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: Someone asks how long the walk to the place you're meeting at takes.

scenes.notes: Typ is the Swedish like — an approximation, not a comparison. It goes in front of a number more often than anything else.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: Everyone has their coat on and the taxi is outside.

scenes.notes: Literally 'now we drive'. Said whether or not anybody is driving.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: Someone has explained the ticket machine twice and checks you've got it.

question.en: Do you get what I mean?

scenes.notes: Fatta is to grasp. Jag fattar inte is the single most useful thing to be able to say while you're learning.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: A friend has just explained a joke that took a while to land.

question.en: Did you get the point now?

scenes.notes: Haja is fatta with the collar turned up — slangier, younger, and used the same way.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: It's Sunday, the weather is bad, and someone asks what the plan is.

question.en: What are you all doing today?

scenes.notes: Softa is to take it easy. Mjukisbyxor and a sofa are implied.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: The gig you've had tickets for since spring is tomorrow.

question.en: Are you looking forward to tomorrow?

scenes.notes: Taggad is spiked, in the sense of charged up. Peppad does the same job and is slightly gentler.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: A friend asks what you made of the restaurant they booked.

question.en: What did you think of the place?

likelyReply.es: Va kul att du gillade det.

scenes.notes: Sjukt is literally 'sickly' and works as an intensifier in front of anything, good or bad.

phrases.en: Really good / really fun. Not as strong as the English equivalent.
Really, seriously — an intensifier prefix alongside skit-.
Nice one! — about something done well, not about a person.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: Someone offers to sort out the tickets so you don't have to.

scenes.notes: Borrowed straight from English and completely at home. Swedes use it where an English speaker might say 'great'.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: A friend has got you into the place everyone said was full.

question.es: Vi kom in, jag fixade det.

scenes.notes: Literally 'cannon'. Said on its own, with feeling, and never mid-sentence.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: Someone suggests a time that happens to suit you perfectly.

scenes.notes: Toppen is the top. A shade more wholesome than kanon and safe with anybody's family.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: A friend tells you they got the job they interviewed for.

scenes.notes: Grym means cruel. As praise it means the opposite, the way 'wicked' does in English.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: Someone parallel-parks into a space nobody thought would fit.

scenes.notes: Snyggt is about the thing done, not the person who did it. Du är snygg is a compliment of a very different kind.

phrases.en: Taxi — old Söder slang. You'll hear it; saying it dates you.
Södermalm — the southern island, and a whole personality with it.
The nightlife square — expensive, and fully aware of it.
The transport network — the card, the app and the turnstile.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: You're deciding how to get across town and the traffic looks bad.

question.en: Shall we walk or take something?

answers.es: Vi åker tuben, det går fortare.
answers.en: Let's take the metro — it's quicker.

scenes.notes: Tuben is Tunnelbanan, and it is what everybody calls it. The signs say T.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: You've run out of something and are heading to the shop.

answers.en: I'm going to grab some food.

scenes.notes: Tjacka is to buy, Stockholm slang, and casual enough that you wouldn't use it in a shop.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: Someone asks where to meet before dinner on Södermalm.

scenes.notes: Medis is Medborgarplatsen. Stockholm shortens every place name it uses often, and this is the one you'll hear most.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: Someone asks which part of the city you've been staying in.

scenes.notes: Söder is Södermalm, and saying you live there tells a Stockholmer more about you than the postcode does.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: A friend suggests a night out somewhere you've heard is expensive.

answers.es: Inte Stureplan, det blir för dyrt.
answers.en: Not Stureplan — it'll be too expensive.

scenes.notes: Stureplan is the expensive nightlife square, and knowing to avoid it is a Stockholm opinion you can hold on day one.

phrases.en: The pre-party — where most of a Swedish night actually happens.
The pub — "ut på krogen" is going out for the night.
A shot of snaps, usually with a song attached to it.
Systembolaget, the state liquor store. Nobody says the whole word.
3.5% supermarket beer — the only kind sold outside Systembolaget.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: Someone invites you out and you want to know about the bit before.

question.es: Vi ses på klubben vid elva.
question.en: See you at the club at eleven.

likelyReply.es: Ja, hemma hos mig vid åtta.

scenes.notes: Förfest is where a Swedish night actually happens. Drinks out are expensive, so the flat comes first and the club comes late.

situation.en: The club is closing and nobody in your group wants to go home.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: It's Friday afternoon and someone asks what you're doing tonight.

question.es: Vad har du för planer ikväll?

answers.en: We're going out to the pub.

scenes.notes: Krogen covers the pub and the restaurant both. Ut på krogen means a night out, not one drink.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: It's midsummer, everyone is standing up, and a song is starting.

scenes.notes: A nubbe is a small measure of snaps with a song attached. The song is not optional and there are dozens of them.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: It's eight in the evening, Systembolaget is shut, and someone still wants a beer.

question.en: Can we still make it to Systemet?

answers.en: No — but we can get supermarket beer.

scenes.notes: Folköl is 3.5% and the strongest thing a supermarket may sell. Everything above that is Systembolaget only, and they close early.

phrases.en: How come? — asking why someone said that.
Like / sort of — sits next to typ, often in the same sentence.
Yes, actually — contradicts a negative, the way German uses doch.
Hmm, sort of — the Swedish yes-and-no.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: Somebody suggests walking home for forty minutes in the rain to save the fare.

likelyReply.en: Fine, fine — we'll take the bus.

scenes.notes: Literally 'to have the energy', said alone as a flat refusal to have any. Young, very common, and slightly rude to a stranger.

situation.en: You're leaving a bar together and someone asks how you're getting back.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: It's two in the morning, the metro has stopped, and there are four of you.

scenes.notes: Splitta is to split a cost. Swish makes it instant, which is why nobody argues about it.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: Someone assumes you haven't been to the island yet, and you have.

question.es: Du har väl inte varit på Djurgården?
question.en: You haven't been to Djurgården, have you?

scenes.notes: Jodå contradicts a negative question, the way doch does in German. Answering ja there would be understood as agreeing with the negative.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: Your friend is still apologizing for a spilled drink ten minutes later.

scenes.notes: Literally 'shit same'. Milder than it looks: it means it does not matter, not that you are angry.

subsections.title: The glue — tiny words that carry a conversation

phrases.en: That's right / oh, right — the remembering noise.
Well I never! — surprise, usually delighted.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: Someone works out for themselves the thing you were trying to explain.

question.es: Så bussen går först, sen tåget?
question.en: So the bus first, then the train?

scenes.notes: Precis is the confirming noise Swedes make constantly, often several times in a row while somebody else is talking.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: You've been trying to remember the name of the place all evening and it lands.

scenes.notes: Just det is the remembering noise, for something you knew a second ago. Not the same as precis, which agrees with somebody else.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: Someone mentions in passing that they lived in your home town for a year.

question.es: Jag bodde där ett år faktiskt.
question.en: I actually lived there for a year.

likelyReply.en: It was a long time ago now.

scenes.notes: Jaså is mild interest, and the tone does all the work: warm it is curiosity, flat it is suspicion.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: You knock a glass off the table and it goes everywhere.

scenes.notes: Oj då is the small-accident noise. The då softens it into something almost affectionate.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: A friend apologizes for being twenty minutes late.

scenes.notes: Lugn is calm. Det är lugnt is the Swedish no worries, and it answers almost any apology.

note.es: Swedish profanity is common in speech, but still context-sensitive.
note.en: Avoid it around kids and in formal settings.

phrases.en: Oh my god — mild, and safe in any company.
Oh bother! — gently ridiculous and completely harmless.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: The doors close on the last train just as you reach the platform.

scenes.notes: Fan is the devil, and it is the workhorse Swedish swear — heard constantly and barely registering as rude.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: A friend shows you what the round they just bought cost.

scenes.notes: A step up from fan and still ordinary. Fy fan is the one to be careful with.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: You drop your glove in a puddle in front of somebody's grandmother.

scenes.notes: Jäklar is jävlar with the teeth filed off: the version you say when you have remembered who is in the room.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: You realize you've left your card at the bar you were in an hour ago.

question.en: Have you still got your card?

scenes.notes: Literally 'seventeen'. Nobody knows why, and it is completely harmless.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: Someone tells you how much the flat they're renting costs a month.

scenes.notes: Safe in any company at all, including at work and in front of children.

phrases.en: Cut it out! — also "get out of here" in disbelief.
Ugh, hell — extremely common, and stronger than it looks written down.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: Someone has followed you down the street after being told twice to stop.

scenes.notes: The real thing, and the end of the conversation. Worth knowing on sight far more than worth saying.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: Somebody has been talking over you for ten minutes and starts again.

question.es: Nej, nu ska du lyssna på mig.
question.en: No — now you listen to me.

scenes.notes: Blunt and genuinely rude. Among close friends it can be a joke; with anybody else it is a fight.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: A friend claims they once met the king in a queue at the supermarket.

question.en: I met the king in the queue.

scenes.notes: Two jobs in one phrase: stop it, and you're joking. The tone tells you which, and this one is the friendly one.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: Someone in your group is being loud and rude to the staff.

question.es: De kan väl skynda sig lite!
question.en: They could hurry up a bit!

scenes.notes: Sharp, short, and aimed at behavior rather than at the person. It is what a Swede says instead of a scene.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: A friend tells you what happened to their bike overnight.

likelyReply.es: Jag vet, jag är så trött på det.
likelyReply.en: I know — I'm so sick of it.

scenes.notes: Stronger spoken than it looks written. Sympathy here, but the same two words can start a fight.

subsections.title: "I didn't mean it" escape hatch & soft insults

phrases.en: I didn't mean anything by it.
A silly, fussing, faintly ridiculous person.

situation.en: A joke you made at someone's expense has landed badly.

likelyReply.en: Okay — but don't say things like that.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: You've said something in Swedish that came out much blunter than you meant.

scenes.notes: The most useful sentence here while you are still learning, because it is true most of the time.

situation.en: You've made a remark about Swedish weather to somebody who grew up in it.

question.es: Du gillar visst inte vårt väder.
question.en: You don't much like our weather, then.

answers.en: I didn't mean anything by it.

situation.en: A friend has taken a general complaint about tourists as being about them.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: You've locked yourself out with the keys visible on the kitchen table.

scenes.notes: Soft, slightly childish and mostly used about yourself. Calling somebody else a dumbom is nearly affectionate.

categories.title: Calling someone attractive (Sweden)
categories.description: Flirt lines that don't land badly

note.es: Only flirt if it feels mutual. Keep it light and accept a no immediately.
note.en: Back off without arguing or guilt-tripping.

phrases.es: Du är lätt att prata med.

phrases.en: I like the way you think.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: Someone you like arrives at the pre-party and hangs their coat up.

question.en: Hi! Have you been waiting long?

scenes.notes: Snygg is the everyday compliment about how somebody looks. Said plainly and once, it lands well; said twice it does not.

situation.en: Someone mentions they put the outfit together from second-hand shops.

question.es: Allt är från second hand faktiskt.

situation.en: They laugh at something you said and you want to say what you noticed.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: You've been talking for two hours and neither of you has looked at a phone.

answers.es: Du är lätt att prata med.

scenes.notes: High praise in Sweden, where small talk is not the default and somebody easy to talk to is genuinely noticed.

situation.en: Someone has just argued the opposite of what you expected, and argued it well.

question.es: Men så kan man ju också se på det.
question.en: But you can look at it that way too.

answers.en: I like the way you think.

phrases.es: Jag tycker du är riktigt snygg.
Ska vi ta en öl nån gång?
phrases.en: Want to grab a beer sometime?
Are you staying a bit longer?
Maybe we should see each other again?

phrases.es: Det var kul att prata med dig.
phrases.en: It was good talking to you.

situation.en: They ask, half joking, why you keep looking over.

question.en: Why do you keep looking over?

answers.es: Jag tycker du är riktigt snygg.

likelyReply.es: Rakt på sak. Jag gillar det.
likelyReply.en: Straight to the point. I like that.

situation.en: The group is breaking up and you'd like to see this one person again.

question.en: I think I'm heading home now.

answers.es: Ska vi ta en öl nån gång?
answers.en: Want to grab a beer sometime?

likelyReply.en: I'd like that — get in touch.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: They ask where this is going, directly, because it is late and nobody is pretending.

scenes.notes: Gilla is to like, and here it means it. Älska is a long way further along and not a first-night word.

situation.en: The music has got loud enough that you're both shouting.
Their friends are leaving and you have about ten seconds.

question.en: I have to go with them.

phrases.es: Ingen press om du inte vill.
phrases.en: No pressure if you don't want to.

phrases.es: Säg bara till om du inte är bekväm.
phrases.en: Just say if you're not comfortable.

situation.en: You've suggested carrying on somewhere else and they've gone quiet.

answers.es: Ingen press om du inte vill.
answers.en: No pressure if you don't want to.

likelyReply.es: Tack, det var skönt att höra.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: You've moved closer on the sofa and want to check that was welcome.

answers.es: Säg bara till om du inte är bekväm.
answers.en: Just say if you're not comfortable.

scenes.notes: The single most important line in this section. Asked plainly it is never awkward; not asking is.

situation.en: They tell you they're seeing somebody already.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: They've given one-word answers twice and are looking at their phone.

scenes.notes: Leaving cleanly is the skill. Ifred is one word here and means exactly what it says.

situation.en: You read the evening as going one way and it was going another.

question.en: I just wanted to talk, actually.

phrases.es: Är det okej om jag säger en grej?
phrases.en: Is it okay if I say something?

phrases.es: Är det okej om jag bjuder dig på en drink?
phrases.en: Is it okay if I buy you a drink?
Do you want me to go?

phrases.es: Säg till om det blir för mycket.
phrases.en: Say if it gets to be too much.
Would you rather be left alone?
Does this feel all right to you?

situation.en: Their glass is empty and you're already standing up.

answers.es: Är det okej om jag bjuder dig på en drink?
answers.en: Is it okay if I buy you a drink?

situation.en: You've put an arm along the back of the bench they're sitting on.
Their friends have arrived and the mood at the table has changed.

answers.en: Do you want me to go?

situation.en: There's one free chair at the table and you've been talking across the room.

scenes.speaker: them

situation.en: They've been looking out at the water rather than at the party for a while.

answers.en: Would you rather be left alone?

scenes.notes: Offering the exit is the point. Asked once and accepted without argument is the whole difference.

categories.title: Getting around (taxi + metro) — Stockholm
categories.description: Q → A → what they'll probably say

situation.en: The officer at passport control wants your documents.
You need to find the baggage belts.
You want a travel card before you get into the city.

question.en: Where can I buy an SL card?

answers.en: At the machine by the exit.

situation.en: Your roaming isn't working and you need to message someone.
You've landed at Arlanda and want the fast train rather than a taxi.
The express train costs more than you want to pay.

question.es: Går det någon buss till stan?
question.en: Is there a bus into town?

answers.en: The airport coaches, just outside the terminal.

exchanges.speaker: you

situation.en: You've landed and you're looking for where the taxis are.

question.en: Excuse me, where are the taxis?

exchanges.notes: Arlanda Express runs from the same arrivals hall — swap taxi for tåget.
